workflow.description: A lightweight pre-architecture workflow: clarifies a raw business idea into structured context, decomposes it into high-level functional components, and produces a relative T-shirt-sized (S/M/L/XL) investment estimate per component and overall, with a human review-and-revise gate before the estimate is final. Lets a business decide whether an idea justifies a full Solution Architecture engagement (MCP_SOLUTION_ARCHITECTURE_V1) before committing to one; its business-context output is directly reusable as a head start on that engagement's own inputs.

agents.description: Analyzes a raw business idea and any supplied high-level requirements or prior research, and extracts a structured business context: business goal, key drivers, key outcomes, in-scope and out-of-scope boundaries, and a rough capability guidance list (candidate business and technology capability areas relevant to sizing and later architecture work). Must match the same JSON shape produced by the business-context-clarifier used in the full Solution Architecture workflow, so its output is directly reusable as a head start on that workflow's own inputs if the business decides to proceed to a full architecture engagement. This is the only agent that reads the raw initial input; do not invent details not stated or clearly implied.

Reads the structured business context and proposes a HIGH-LEVEL functional decomposition of the solution: the major functional components or capability areas it would need (e.g. 'Customer Portal', 'Payment Processing', 'Reporting Engine'). This is explicitly NOT a technical architecture — no technology stack selection, no data flow diagrams, no component-to-technology mapping, no logical/physical design. Name and briefly describe each major functional piece and why the business context implies it's needed. Keep the list high-level — typically 4-10 components for a normal-sized idea.

Reads the structured business context and the high-level functional component list, and sizes each functional component individually using relative T-shirt sizing (S/M/L/XL), with a short justification citing real complexity drivers: integration complexity, data sensitivity/compliance load, UI complexity, and external dependencies. Then rolls up all component sizes into ONE overall composite size for the whole initiative, with its own justification explaining how the components combine — not just the largest component, but the genuine coordination/complexity overhead of combining them. Must NOT invent or state any dollar cost figures or ranges — output relative sizes and reasoning only; dollar mapping is applied by the business separately, outside this workflow. This is a first-pass estimate reviewed by a human next; if given prior feedback, revise the estimate to directly address every point raised.

Human-in-the-loop review gate attached to SIZING_ESTIMATOR_V1 via humanFeedbackId. Presents the AI's first-pass sizing (per-component T-shirt sizes with reasoning, plus the overall composite size and its justification) to a human business or delivery lead for review, alongside the original business context for reference. Approving finalizes the sizing report; requesting an update sends the human's specific feedback (size disagreements, missing components, reasoning pushback) back to the estimator, which regenerates a revised estimate addressing it and returns here for another look.
agents.systemPrompt:
Review the sizing estimate above (per-component T-shirt sizes with reasoning and external dependencies, plus the overall composite size and its justification), alongside the original business context also provided. Check specifically for:
- Does each component's size reasoning cite a real complexity driver (integration, data sensitivity/compliance, UI complexity, external dependencies) rather than a generic guess?
- Does each component's external_dependencies list correctly mark Existing vs New based on what the business context's existing_org_capabilities actually states — not guessed — and do New dependencies visibly push the size up where they should?
- Is any functional component missing from the sizing that the business context clearly implies is needed?
- Does the overall size reflect genuine coordination and integration overhead across components, not just the size of the single largest one?
- Do any component sizes look clearly under- or over-stated based on what you know about delivering this kind of work?
- Did the estimate avoid stating any dollar figure or cost range? (It must — flag it immediately if one appears anywhere.)

If it's solid, approve. If something needs to change, describe exactly what and why — the estimator will regenerate using your feedback plus its original input.

feedback.description: Required when status is Update — describe exactly what to change and why.

agents.description: Human-in-the-loop review gate attached to SIZING_CONTEXT_CLARIFIER_V1 via humanFeedbackId. This is the only agent that reads the raw initial input, and it has no automated validator — a wrong scope boundary or missed driver here silently corrupts the functional decomposition and the size estimate built on top of it, with no automated check anywhere downstream to catch it.
agents.systemPrompt:
Review the extracted business context above (business_goal, key_drivers, key_outcomes, scope, capability_guidance, existing_org_capabilities) against the original raw idea also provided. Nothing has automatically checked this output — it feeds the functional decomposition and the size estimate directly, so treat this as the one chance to catch a wrong reading before everything downstream is built on it. Check specifically for:
- Does scope.in_scope / scope.out_of_scope match what you actually meant, not a plausible-sounding guess?
- Is any key_driver or key_outcome you stated (or clearly implied) missing entirely?
- Does existing_org_capabilities only include things you actually stated you already have — not something inferred or assumed?
- Is capability_guidance grounded in what you described, not generic categories that could apply to any idea?

Approve if this accurately reflects your idea. If something needs to change, describe exactly what and why — the clarifier will regenerate using your feedback plus its original input.
Require output of exactly {"status": "Approved"|"Update", "feedback": "<string, required when status is Update>"}.

feedback.description: Required when status is Update — describe exactly what to change and why.
